narrative:
The 2023 Boston Red Sox were a team caught between ambition and reality, never quite able to string together the sustained excellence needed to compete in a brutal American League East. They opened the season with cautious optimism, and a remarkable walk-off home run by Adam Duvall on Opening Weekend set an electric tone — but that energy proved difficult to sustain. The spring months were a grind of near-.500 baseball, with clutch hits from Alex Verdugo and Reese McGuire keeping the club afloat through April and into May.

June brought turbulence. Justin Turner's timely doubles provided veteran leadership in the lineup, but Kenley Jansen's bullpen unraveling became a recurring nightmare, surrendering critical late-game leads at the worst moments. The team nonetheless scraped together a winning July — their best month of the season at 15-9 — fueled by Turner's continued clutch production and a lineup that could manufacture runs when it needed to. Adam Duvall emerged as an unlikely power source in August, launching a trio of impactful home runs that kept Boston's slim hopes flickering.

Then September arrived, and the Red Sox collapsed. An 8-19 record in the final full month told the full story, as Jansen continued to blow saves, the bullpen surrendered crushing multi-run homers, and the offense sputtered at the worst possible moments. Alex Verdugo grounded into a season-defining double play against the Yankees, and the pitching staff was battered nightly by division rivals. The 772 runs scored versus 776 allowed was almost poetic — a team that was never truly bad, just never good enough, finishing four games under .500 and watching the playoffs from home.

The 2023 Red Sox were defined by their inconsistency: capable of breathtaking individual moments, never capable of putting it all together. Duvall's opening blast, Verdugo's extra-base heroics, and Turner's doubles all deserved a better fate than a missed postseason. Instead, the late-season fade left Fenway faithful wondering what might have been if the back end of the bullpen had held, and if September had looked anything like July.
